text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Political parties are falling out over the nuclear power debate with the Green Party thrown out of ongoing talks about when the country's nuclear industry will be closed down. The Centre party is continuing talks but on the condition that the first nuclear power stations will be closed in 1998.
- Insurer Skandia gives up the fight for mortgage bank Stadshypotek. Shareholders are recommended to accept the rival bid by Handelsbanken.

- Sales of tabloid paper Expressen fell 18.8 percent in November this year compared to a year ago with only 331,700 readers. Rival paper Aftonbladet took over as biggest selling paper with 399,100 readers in November which was an 8.1 percent rise from last year.

- Inflation is under control, according to the central bank's fourth and final report for the year. The report painted a bright picture for the future saying it was more optimistic than even three months ago. It forecast the inflation rate at 1.5 percent in 1997 and two percent in 1998.
- Yet another party, the Greens, is out of the negotiations regarding the future of nuclear power in Sweden.
- Insurance company Skandia has withdrawn from the battle for mortgage bank Stadshypotek.
- Purchases of used company cars, household heating oil and alcohol lifted private consumption in the third quarter.
- Temporary factors are behind low inflation in Sweden.
- The Scandic hotel chain's debut on the Stockholm bourse was successful, with shares closing 8.5 crowns above its introductory price at 103.5 crowns.
- A price war over insurance for companies saw insurance premiums drop by up to 50 percent this year and more falls are likely in 1997.
- Sydkraft won the fight over Orebro Energi and announced it would buy the company for 2.3 billion crowns. This is the biggest acquisition this year for a local energy company.

- Heads of three competing forestry products trade houses -- Ekmans, Cellmark and Elof Hansson -- are tempted by the adventure involved in becoming listed companies. Ekmans is due to be listed in 1998. This will open ownership opportunities in a sector of Swedish industry unknown before to the public.

- Astra is having a hard time convincing analysts about the firm's prospects when the patent for blockbusting anti-ulcer drug Losec expires, a stock market commentator writes. The risk in the share right now is higher than usual.

- Managing director of Swedish camera company Hasselblad Staffan Junel will resign. Newspaper sources say the company's new owners Union Bank of Switzerland would like to concentrate on conventional camera models instead of digital ones.
